title: Ofuta
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Dried bean pods and banana peelings burnt to ash, the ash mixed with water and sieved into a brown liquid — added early to greens so they keep their chlorophyll colour.
longDesc: Ofuta is a cooking liquid made from ash, and it does a job that cooks everywhere want done: it keeps boiled greens green. You burn dried bean pods and banana peelings, mix the ash with water, sieve it, and the brown liquid goes into the pot early. The Lugbara use it for greens like osubi, the bean leaves, and it is one of three alkaline preparations in their kitchen. Nobody outside West Nile seems to write this down.
steps: Burn the dried bean pods and banana peelings to ash.
Sieve it to produce a brown liquid.
Add it early to the pot when cooking greens like osubi, so they keep their green chlorophyll colour.
chefTips: Add it early, not late. It goes in at the start of the boil, which is when it can protect the chlorophyll.
Sieve it properly. Ash particles left in are gritty and will spoil the dish.
Dried bean pods and banana peelings — both are kitchen waste, which is the point. This costs nothing.
It is an alkaline liquid and a little goes a long way. Too much and greens go slippery and soapy.

Two related Lugbara preparations do adjacent jobs: a'itipa, UGA098, is a salt from burnt salty leaves, and magadi is a mineral salt from saline water. Either can be added early for the same colour-keeping effect.

The Lugbara cooking philosophy on boiling is worth having in full: boiling takes away the sharp juicy taste, so ofutaku, magadi or a'itipa go in early to keep the leaves green, and sweeteners — avocado, kamura odu which is oil from a tree's bark, and sesame oil — are added at the table afterwards.
No quantities are documented for this or for any of the ash preparations. Nothing has been estimated.
commonMistakes: Adding it at the end of cooking.
Using too much, which turns greens soapy.
Burning treated or painted material for the ash.
Storing it in a metal container, which it will attack.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which describes ofuta or ofutaku as produced by burning dried bean pods, banana peelings and similar material and mixing the ash with water before sieving to produce a brown liquid used to cook greens like osubi, and which states that it maintains their green chlorophyll colour.

That article's boiling philosophy is reproduced closely: although the sharp juicy taste is taken away by boiling, ofutaku, magadi or a'itipa can be added early to maintain the green colour of the leaves, while sweeteners such as avocado, kamura odu — edible oil from the bark of a certain tree — and sesame oil are added at the table.

That article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material on Lugbara culture, so its taxonomy is treated here as a lead list rather than as established fact. No quantities are given anywhere in it.
storage: Keeps indefinitely in a sealed glass or plastic jar.
healthBenefits: Adds potassium and trace minerals from the plant ash.
Helps retain the chlorophyll and some of the water-soluble vitamins in boiled greens.
Contains no fat, sugar or sodium of its own.
culturalNote: Alkaline cooking liquids made from plant ash turn up across Africa and in Mexican nixtamalisation, and they are one of the oldest chemistry tricks in cooking. That the Lugbara have three of them — an ash liquid, an ash salt and a mineral salt — and distinguish between them is knowledge held entirely in a language with very little written about its food.
